newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Iliescu urges Romanians to back his re-election.
newsitem.headline: Iliescu urges Romanians to back his re-election.

text.p: President Ion Iliescu told Romanians on Wednesday that only he could prevent instability and urged them to support his re-election bid against a reformist whose bloc triumphed in parliamentary polls.

Iliescu, in power since the 1989 collapse of communism, conceded that his left-wing Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) had lost its grip on power in Sunday's ballot to the opposition Democratic Convention (CDR) bloc of Emil Constantinescu.
The Convention announced it was on the brink of clinching an agreement to lead a coalition government with former prime minister Petre Roman's Social Democrats (USD).
Iliescu, who led in the first round of the presidential vote also held on Sunday, vowed not to obstruct government if he won the run-off against Constantinescu on November 17.
"Political reality makes my presence as head of state more necessary than ever before," Iliescu told a news conference.

"I will not hinder the new government and the new parliamentary majority. On the contrary, I'll support them to achieve their programmes as long as they are to the benefit of the country and do not threaten social stability."
Near-final results of the presidential vote gave Iliescu 32 percent, four points more than Constantinescu. Former prime minister Petre Roman was third on 21 percent.
Constantinescu, a professor with no political career under Communist rule, and Roman have stayed out of the limelight, while their parties fine-tuned a coalition accord.

Officials of both parties said the leaders would sign a deal on Thursday. They suggested it would also involve Roman throwing his support behind Constantinescu in the second round of the presidential vote.
Iliescu, a former communist, appointed Roman his prime minister after they both swept to power in the violent 1989 upheaval which ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
But Roman was ousted within two years after riots led by vigilante coal miners, which he later blamed on Iliescu.

Iliescu, 66, had suggested that the opposition talks were not going well. He challenged the Convention to live up to promises to improve living standards under a "Contract with Romania" it promoted during the campaign.
"I hope there will be a smooth transition from one government to another," he said. "The situation requires that a new government should be formed immediately."
The president said his re-election would counter "radical voices" within the Convention, an apparent jibe at a handful of monarchists seeking the return of exiled former King Michael.
He also suggested other CDR factions, representing 60,000 Communist-era prisoners, might unleash anti-communist purges. Both themes were vote-winners in 1990 and 1992 elections.

"I am the guarantee that issues raised over the past few years will not happen -- changing the system of government ...restrictions against former Communist Party members, or political purges in the administration," he said.

Unofficial results showed that Iliescu had won a seat in parliament for the PDSR -- a political safety net if he loses the run-off. Most of Prime minister Nicolae Vacaroiu's cabinet ministers also won seats.
